sentences.text: Its teeth were nearly conical with distinct unserrated edges on both the front and back. The upper jaw tip held four teeth on each side, while the main jaw bones carried twelve or thirteen teeth each.
The thigh bones were slender, and the animal had bony scutes covering both its back and belly. The scutes on the back were arranged in two rows that ran the full length of the animal.
The fossil remains of Kayentasuchus were discovered in 1983 by paleontologist James M. Clark at Willow Springs, located 50 kilometers northeast of Flagstaff.

The skeleton was discovered in channel sandstone within the silty facies of the Kayenta Formation. Fossils of the turtle Kayentachelys, the dinosaur Scutellosaurus, and tritylodonts were found nearby just meters below the Kayentasuchus skeleton.
The genus Kayentasuchus was formally named in 2002 by James M. Clark and Hans-Dieter Sues. The type species, K. walkeri, was named in honor of the paleontologist Alick Walker.
Kayentasuchus is a genus of sphenosuchian, a basal member of the crocodylomorph clade that includes crocodilians and their closest relatives.
Phylogenetic analysis places Kayentasuchus in an unresolved position among sphenosuchians, distinct from both true crocodiles and the genus Sphenosuchus.
Kayentasuchus lived between 199.5 and 184.2 million years ago during the Sinemurian to Pliensbachian stages.
